t.3.6.1: But Rāma, the scorcher of foes, accompanied by his brother and by Sītā, went to the hermitage of Sutīkṣṇa together with those twice-born sages.
t.3.6.2: Having travelled a long way and crossed rivers full of water, he beheld a vast mountain, lofty like a great cloud.
t.3.6.3: Then those two Rāghavas, the best of the Ikṣvākus, together with Sītā, entered that forest, filled throughout with trees of many kinds.
t.3.6.4: Having entered the dreadful forest, rich in trees laden with many flowers and fruits, he saw in a secluded spot a hermitage adorned with rows of bark garments.
t.3.6.5: There Rāma duly addressed the ascetic Sutīkṣṇa, who was seated, bearing matted locks smeared with dirt and mud, and grown great in austerity.
t.3.6.6: I am Rāma, O blessed one, and I have come to see you. Therefore speak to me, O knower of dharma, O great seer, whose valor is truth.
t.3.6.7: Then, having looked upon the heroic Rāma, the foremost of those who uphold dharma, and having embraced him with both arms, he spoke these words.
t.3.6.8: Welcome indeed to you, O hero Rāma, best of those who uphold dharma! Now that you have set foot in it, this hermitage has, as it were, found its protector.
t.3.6.9: Waiting for you alone, O greatly renowned one, I do not ascend from here to the world of the gods, O hero, casting off my body upon the surface of the earth.
t.3.6.11: In those worlds frequented by the divine sages, which I have won through my austerity, may you, by my grace, roam at your pleasure together with your wife and with Lakṣmaṇa.
t.3.6.10: I had heard that you, Kākutstha, deprived of your kingdom, had made Citrakūṭa your dwelling and come here. Śatakratu, the king of the gods, came here and told me that all the worlds have been won by me through my meritorious deeds.
t.3.6.12: To that radiant great sage of fierce austerities, a speaker of truth, the self-possessed Rāma replied, as Vāsava replies to Brahmā.
t.3.6.13: I myself shall win those worlds by my own effort, O great sage; but I wish for a dwelling place to be pointed out to me here in this forest.
t.3.6.15: Thus addressed by Rāma, the great sage renowned throughout the world, flooded with great joy, spoke sweet words.
t.3.6.14: Your honour, who are skilled in every respect and devoted to the welfare of all beings, has been spoken of by the great-souled Śarabhaṅga Gautama.
t.3.6.16: This very hermitage, O Rāma, is excellent; may you take your delight here. It is frequented by hosts of sages and is always furnished with roots and fruits.
t.3.6.17: O illustrious one, herds of deer come to this hermitage, roam about, and after tempting us they go back again, fearing nothing from any quarter.
t.3.6.18: Having heard those words of the great sage, the steadfast elder brother of Lakṣmaṇa drew his bow fitted with an arrow and spoke these words.
t.3.6.19: O most illustrious one, I might slay those herds of deer that gather here with an arrow whose edge is keen and whose splendour is like the thunderbolt.
t.3.6.21: Having spoken thus to that granter of boons, Rāma went to perform the twilight rite. Having observed the evening twilight worship, he made his dwelling there for the night.
t.3.6.20: Your honor would then be caught up in offense; what could be more grievous than that? Therefore I do not consider it fitting to dwell long in this hermitage.
t.3.6.22: Then, when the twilight rites were done and he saw that night had come, the great-souled Sutīkṣṇa, having honoured them well, himself gave to those two bulls among men the auspicious food fit for ascetics.
